scenes.narration: In 2022, we came to Canada from Ukraine with two kids. And almost all the money we had went into an old car.
scenes.visual: Roman Financial family arriving in Canada with luggage beside an older used car.

scenes.narration: Not a dream car. Not the car you put in a thumbnail and pretend life is perfect. Just an old car that could take us to work, to school, to groceries, and hopefully not surprise us too often.
scenes.visual: Older used car as practical newcomer lifeline: work, school, groceries, repairs.

scenes.narration: We were renting. We had left our apartment back home. And then I started looking at houses. Eight hundred thousand dollars. Nine hundred thousand. Sometimes one million. I remember looking at those numbers and thinking, this is not difficult. This is impossible.
scenes.visual: Family in rental kitchen facing abstract housing prices, laptop lid facing viewer only.

scenes.narration: And that feeling matters, because a lot of people talk about money like it is just math. But when you arrive in a new country, money is not only math. Money is language. Rules. Credit history. Tax accounts. Rent. Insurance. A car you need before you even understand what the car really costs.
scenes.visual: Newcomer surrounded by abstract systems: language, rules, credit, taxes, rent, insurance, car costs.

scenes.narration: And on top of that, you are still building normal life. Kids need stability. Groceries still need to be bought. The rent does not care that you are new here.
scenes.visual: Family groceries, rent keys, school bags, normal life pressure in warm apartment scene.

scenes.narration: So this is not a video about how we became rich. We did not. This is not a video about which stock you should buy, or which ETF is perfect, or whether you should buy a house tomorrow. This is a personal story about how we went from zero down payment to having options.
scenes.visual: Roman speaking honestly at kitchen table, no guru pose, family context behind him.

scenes.narration: And honestly, options are underrated. Because when you have no options, every price looks like a wall. When you start building capital, even slowly, the same world begins to look like a map.
scenes.visual: Wall of prices transforming into a map of possible paths.

scenes.narration: Back in Ukraine, we had never really invested. About a year before moving, I had only a couple thousand dollars to experiment with. That was it. No deep experience. No magic strategy. No secret rich uncle explaining compound interest over dinner.
scenes.visual: Roman as beginner with small experiment account, humble notes, no magic shortcut.

scenes.narration: So when we arrived in Canada, I started researching like someone who was already late. I wanted to understand the system. Not perfectly. Just enough to stop feeling completely blind.
scenes.visual: Late-night research desk with Roman learning Canadian finance basics.

scenes.narration: What is a broker? What account should I open? What is the difference between saving and investing? Why does everyone talk about taxes? Why does credit score suddenly matter so much? What is employer matching? What is cashback? Why does every bank have three products that sound almost the same?
scenes.visual: Abstract question cloud of brokers, accounts, taxes, credit, employer match, cashback, banks.

scenes.narration: It was a lot. And at the beginning, the more I learned, the more behind I felt. That is one of the strange parts of immigration. You can be a capable adult, but the financial system can make you feel like a beginner again.
scenes.visual: Capable adult standing before a maze of finance rules, feeling like a beginner.

scenes.narration: But eventually, I found a useful idea. You do not need to understand everything to start. You need to understand enough to start safely.
scenes.visual: Simple first step over a confusing finance maze, calm practical breakthrough.

scenes.narration: For investing, one of those beginner-friendly tools was ETFs. An ETF is basically a basket. Instead of trying to pick one perfect company, you can buy a basket that owns many companies inside it. That does not mean it is risk free. It is still investing. The value can go down. But the idea is simple enough for a beginner to understand.
scenes.visual: ETF basket metaphor with many company blocks, risk shown gently as waves under the basket.

scenes.narration: And simple matters when your life is already full. I personally became interested in investing. I liked reading about companies. So for my own accounts, I bought individual stocks. My wife did not want to do that. And that is completely reasonable. Not everyone wants to spend their evenings reading earnings reports. Some people have healthier hobbies. Apparently.
scenes.visual: Two paths: Roman researching stocks, wife choosing a calmer simple investing path.

scenes.narration: So for her accounts, I chose the simpler ETF-style path. Baskets instead of stock picking. Same family goal. Different level of complexity. That became one of the first lessons for us: the best system is not the most impressive system. The best system is the one the person can actually keep using.
scenes.visual: Wife's simple ETF basket path moving toward family stability.

scenes.narration: After rent, insurance, the old car, groceries, kids, phone bills, and all the normal expenses, we did not have some huge amount left over. But we decided to invest one hundred and fifty dollars a week. That was less than I could make in a day.
scenes.visual: Family budget table with expenses and one small weekly investment contribution.

scenes.narration: And when you compare one hundred and fifty dollars to a house that costs eight hundred thousand, it feels almost ridiculous. Like trying to fight a forest fire with a water bottle. At the beginning, it felt pointless.
scenes.visual: Tiny contribution compared to enormous abstract house-price wall, humorous but grounded.

scenes.narration: You put money in. The account still looks small. Then the market moves and sometimes it looks even smaller. Nothing dramatic happens. Nobody claps. You still drive the same old car. You still rent. But this is where the boring part becomes important.
scenes.visual: Same car, same rent, small account slowly moving through ordinary weeks.

scenes.narration: A lot of financial progress does not feel like progress while it is happening. It feels like repetition. Every week, a small amount. Every month, learning one more thing. Every year, a little more confidence.
scenes.visual: Calendar pages, small contributions, learning notes, confidence gradually growing.

scenes.narration: We learned about investment accounts. We learned about brokers. We learned that employer matching can matter. We learned that cashback is not a wealth strategy, but if you are already spending money, you might as well stop leaving small benefits on the table. We learned that credit is not just a score; it affects real options. We learned that taxes are not a topic you can ignore forever.
scenes.visual: Tool stack of accounts, broker, employer match, cashback, credit, taxes.

scenes.narration: Four years later, my investment accounts are around fifty eight thousand six hundred dollars. My wife's accounts are around fifty four thousand five hundred dollars. Together, that is about one hundred and thirteen thousand dollars. These numbers are not here to impress anyone. They are here because they changed the question.
scenes.visual: Two account towers forming a down-payment foundation, personal and not flashy.

scenes.narration: Recently, we saw a similar house near the one we rent listed for around five hundred twenty seven thousand dollars. And for the first time, the question was not, how could we ever buy a home? The question became, should we buy one now, or keep growing?
scenes.visual: Family at a fork: first home path and keep-growing investment path.

scenes.narration: Now, there are important details. Having more than twenty percent of a purchase price does not mean buying is automatically the right decision. There are closing costs. Mortgage payments. Maintenance. Interest rates. Taxes. Opportunity cost. Stability for the family also matters. This is why I do not want this channel to be about pretending money decisions are obvious.
scenes.visual: House decision scale balancing costs, mortgage, maintenance, rates, taxes, opportunity, stability.

scenes.narration: So the lesson from our first four years is not, copy us. The lesson is this. If you are starting from zero in a new country, the first goal is not to look rich. The first goal is to understand the system well enough to build options. That is what this channel is about. Money after immigration. The mistakes. The tools. The accounts. The car decisions. The house decisions. The investing path. Four years ago, we did not even have the question. And that is the change. We went from zero to options.
scenes.visual: Warm montage of Roman Financial journey: family, car, rent, accounts, investing, house decision, path forward.
